production.text: Luster-painted pottery required specialized surface techniques; the selected vessel is attributed to Iraq.

evidence.text: Samarra’s archaeology is particularly important because early Baghdad survives unevenly.

coordination.text: Craft production and book copying require organized skill and resources, while court locations and effective political control change over time.

name: Abbasid Iraq: cities, surfaces and changing power
geographicPrecision: Baghdad locator; Samarra lies north along the Tigris. No fixed caliphal boundary.

interval.label: Abbasid rule in Baghdad: conventional frame, 750–1258 CE
interval.note: Baghdad founded 762; court at Samarra 836–892. Authority changed substantially; later nominal caliphs in Egypt are outside this frame.

question: Can a craft tradition spread while political unity weakens?
summary: Cities, workshops and books followed different rhythms within Abbasid-era Iraq. A bowl makes skilled surface work visible, while its unknown workshop remains a question. Baghdad’s founding, the court’s move to Samarra and later changes in political control did not make one continuous administrative system. Reading craft beside urban and scholarly institutions gives a fuller history than the dynasty label alone.

sections.title: A capital concentrated demands and opportunities
sections.text: Baghdad was founded in 762, after the Abbasids had taken power in 750. The court moved to Samarra in 836 and returned to Baghdad in 892. Building, supplying and decorating those places created work for many kinds of maker. Yet a find at a palace need not have been produced nearby or commissioned personally by a ruler. The two capitals are separate settings in a longer history, and the wider population’s work cannot be reduced to court consumption.

citations.locator: Capital foundation, moves and archaeological survival

sections.title: The bowl’s surface required decisions and skill
sections.text: The selected tenth-century vessel is earthenware with lustre painting over an opaque white glaze. A seated man, plants and birds organize its decoration; the catalogue reads a blessing on its foot. Making such surfaces involved ingredients, skilled potters, kilns, fuel and attention, including failures. The process diagram separates the ceramic body, glazed surface and controlled lustre firing. It explains a technical task without assigning a recipe, temperature or named workshop to this accession.

citations.locator: Description, medium, inscription and Iraq attribution

sections.title: A production place needs more than a style name
sections.text: Pottery found at Samarra is not automatically pottery made there. Kiln debris and material comparisons provide different evidence from a vessel’s decoration. Petersen’s fieldwork report discusses Basra-region finds while retaining uncertainties about their original recovery and the possibility of several southern Iraqi production centers. Early Basra near al-Zubayr also differs from the modern city farther east. Neither this regional research nor the bowl’s Iraq attribution identifies the selected object’s precise workshop, owner or journey.

sections.title: Books also depended on skilled production
sections.text: A manuscript leaf attributed to Baghdad and dated 621 AH/1224 CE names ‘Abdullah ibn al-Fadl. It belongs to an Arabic version of a much older Greek treatise and combines writing with illustration. This later object makes copying, interpretation and presentation visible. Its date is not the beginning of translation into Arabic, and an illustrated setting is not an observed hospital interior. The example extends the account beyond pottery without treating every city or century as one scholarly institution.

sections.title: Political authority changed before the final date
sections.text: The caliphs’ power narrowed as other rulers gained control; Baghdad’s capture by the Buyids in 945 and Seljuqs in 1055 differs from the Mongol sack in 1258. The conventional endpoint cannot stand in for centuries of unchanged rule. Crafts, books and institutions therefore need their own dated evidence.

claims.text: Baghdad’s 762 foundation and Samarra’s 836–892 capital phase are different from the full dynastic frame.

deeperReading.title: Ordinary pottery broadens the question
deeperReading.text: A 2022 study examined 134 selected common, generally unglazed sherds from Murwab in Qatar. Petrography addresses materials and possible origins; chemical results and provenance suggestions remain preliminary. This concerns a different settlement and different sampled pots, not chemical testing of the selected Met bowl. It shows why an account centered on a glittering museum vessel should also ask about cooking, storage and household supply. The sample does not count every pot or identify the movements of every household.

deeperReading.title: Old explanations remain questions to test
deeperReading.text: Rosser-Owen’s course discusses theories connecting costly innovation with court sponsorship and overseas trade. Petersen’s report explicitly qualifies production-center arguments and warns that collected surface sherds only indicate, rather than securely date, occupation. Keep these kinds of inference visible: a hypothesis about investment, evidence about a clay fabric and an object’s museum attribution do different work. None alone establishes who paid a potter, whether a particular worker migrated or how one vessel reached a consumer.

deeperReading.title: A century-wide object date can cross a political change
deeperReading.text: The selected bowl’s tenth-century date spans the 945 change in Baghdad’s control. That range cannot establish whether it was made before or after the takeover, still less identify a patron from the ruling dynasty. Ask what additional dating or ownership evidence would narrow the question. The manuscript’s 1224 date supplies a different degree of precision for another object and task. A dynastic label groups material for study; it cannot replace the dates and circumstances of manufacture, use and survival.

evidenceReading.title: Do not merge findplace, manufacture and a dynastic name
evidenceReading.introduction: Paraphrases distinguish catalogue attribution, field observations and an independently dated manuscript.

items.label: The vessel has an attribution
items.text: The Met dates 1977.126 to the tenth century and attributes it to Iraq.
items.interpretation: This is broader than a known workshop or excavated palace context. The catalogue locates the blessing on the foot; the two supplied photographs show the decorated interior, not that inscription.

items.label: Fieldwork tests places of production
items.text: Petersen reports kiln-related material and competing production-center interpretations around early Basra.
items.interpretation: Evidence from clay and kilns cannot be transferred automatically to every similar-looking bowl.

items.label: A book has a much later date
items.text: Accession 57.51.21 is dated 1224 CE and attributed to Baghdad.
items.interpretation: A copy/illustration date is distinct from the underlying treatise and earlier translation work. Its pictured activity is not direct observation.

familyActivity.title: Follow the work behind a shining surface
steps: Look at the bowl, then the supplied production diagram. Name one visible decoration.
Point to a step a finished photograph cannot show: preparing material, firing or controlling the kiln.
Say which question needs workshop evidence rather than the photograph.
familyActivity.explanation: The activity distinguishes visible features from inferred production. It supplies no ancient recipe and does not identify the workshop of this particular bowl.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Bounded C5 account with main/deeper/evidence reading, family entry, phased context, sourced geography and modern explanatory media.
limitations: Selected museum objects and reports do not cover Abbasid agriculture, fiscal administration, slave labor, urban conflict or scholarly institutions comprehensively.
Hallett’s thesis, the underlying Basra petrographic datasets and original manuscript text have not been independently reanalysed.
Early Basra topography remains qualified; the source’s modern canals and surface finds do not supply a securely reconstructed ninth-century route.

placeStudy.title: Iraqi settings: two capitals and early Basra
placeStudy.description: City-area locators distinguish court locations and a southern production/research region. The map reconstructs no ancient canal, workshop location, empire boundary or journey of the selected bowl.

points.label: Baghdad — founded in 762
points.text: The capital’s foundation precedes the later manuscript dated 1224. These dates do not describe one unchanged city or institution.

points.label: Samarra — court setting, 836–892
points.text: A phase of court residence differs from the whole Abbasid frame. Finds or styles associated with Samarra need not have been manufactured there.

points.label: Al-Zubayr area — early Basra research
points.text: The deliberately rounded regional point orients Petersen’s early Basra study near al-Zubayr, southwest of the modern city. It is not a particular kiln findspot or precise ancient shoreline.
